done.why: I died a fourth time inside the mirror box in the endgame. I had left the pine panel open and pushed the box north past the guardians, and their bludgeons came through the roof. The old man had already warned me there would be no fourth return, and the game left me in the Void, where it said nothing more would happen.

about: I'm an old adventurer on a last test, set by an old man who turns out to be the Dungeon Master. You collect the things he carries in my dream (staff, ring, book, hood and cloak, an amulet) by being good to people rather than by force: you let a thief rob you, feed a starving old man, steal a ring from history and hide it under a time machine seat, and spare a hooded figure who turns out to have your own face. Under all that, it's a sad tour of a collapsed empire: aqueducts falling apart, a sunlit oasis you can't get up to, museums holding machines that don't work.

ending.what: A losing ending. I reached full potential (7 of 7), went through the secret door, broke the beam with the sword, got the mirror box turned to face north, and was crushed by the guardians' bludgeons because I had opened the pine panel. That was my fourth death, and the voice said goodbye: 'perhaps it has been another that I have been seeking.' I ended in the Void.

moments.note: The lantern as 'an old friend who has followed you somewhere it would rather not have come' set the tone right away.
'Something that is not a tree is keeping very still.' A lovely, creepy way to hint at the man by the cliff.
The chest got hauled up and I was stuck on the ledge. The waits that followed (counting coins, pacing, 'keep your shirt on') made the wait itself into a story.
I fed the waybread to the old man and the secret door showed itself. Satisfying.
The shiny object in the lake slipped out of my hand every time I tried, over three dives here and two more later. I never learned what it wanted from me.
The Scenic Vista table that sends you to whatever it's showing. Clever, and the clues on the can and the table fit together.
I died in the grue lair after using the one spray. Then I found the can was empty for good, so the dark slope was shut to me for the rest of the game.
I came back from 776 and the ring was gone, even though I was wearing it. Fair, but I'd wasted a long trip.
I typed several commands at once, the push east failed because the stone door was closed, and the time machine took me back to a room full of guards. I died a second time.
Flathead's guards planning 'Flood Control Dam #3' and hollowed-out volcanoes. Laughed out loud.
'The ring is concealed underneath the seat', and it was waiting for me back in 948. Best puzzle payoff in the game.
In the Royal Puzzle I pushed the ladder block north without thinking. That locked column 0 for good and trapped me.
Shouting got me the hint 'if you pray enough...', and praying killed me as a way out. I died a third time, and the old man said he had no fourth return in him.
I took the hood off the beaten figure and saw my own face. Chilling.
I pushed the pine wall hoping to move the box, and it just swung open. Nothing warned me that an open panel would be fatal once the box moved.
Bludgeons through the roof, and the run was over at the very end.

wished: I wished I could work out how to actually pick up the shiny object in the lake. Five tries over two dives never got it.
I wished there had been a second dose of grue repellent, or another way up the dark slope south of the lake once the one spray was used.
I wished I could get out of the Royal Puzzle once I'd jammed it, other than by dying.
I wished I knew where my ring went after the third death. I never found it again.
I wished the mirror box had warned me in some way that an open panel was deadly before I pushed it past the guardians.
I wished I could have tried the Flathead Ocean properly; it felt like something should come out of the mist.

lines.line: It has the look of an old friend who has followed you somewhere it would rather not have come.
lines.why: Told me straight away this was a tired, tender farewell kind of adventure.

lines.line: It is the best thing you have seen in three adventures and there is no way to it.
lines.why: The sunlight hole. A whole mood in one sentence.

lines.line: Still there? Good. I said a short while, and a short while is what I meant; keep your shirt on.
lines.why: The thief's voice made waiting on the ledge fun instead of dead time.

lines.line: It is the saddest thing you have seen underground, and you have seen some sad things.
lines.why: The aqueduct. The game kept coming back to the Empire as a ruin.

lines.line: We shall call it ... Flood Control Dam #3.
lines.why: Dimwit Flathead's guards overheard in 776. A joke that pays off a whole series.

lines.line: If you pray enough, it is said down here, your prayers may be answered.
lines.why: The only way out of a jammed puzzle, and it cost me a life.

lines.line: Three times now I have sent you back, my friend, and the power I spend on you is not in endless store; I do not think there is a fourth in me.
lines.why: The old man's warning that the next death was final. It made the stakes real.

lines.line: You slowly remove the hood from your badly wounded opponent and recoil in horror at the sight of your own face, weary and wounded.
lines.why: The emotional peak of the game.

lines.line: I have waited a long age for you, my friend, but perhaps it has been another that I have been seeking. Good night, oh worthy adventurer!
lines.why: A gentle, crushing goodbye at the end.

fun.why: Most puzzles were delightful when they clicked: the chest and rope, feeding the old man, the Vista table, hiding the ring under the seat, sparing the figure. The deaths stung, especially the last one right at the end, and the Royal Puzzle grind wasn't fun.

engagement.why: I always wanted to see the next room, and the dwindling lives pulled me forward. The run through the Royal Puzzle and the repeated lake dives sagged.

difficulty.why: Several things went wrong for good with little warning: one spray of repellent, a ladder block that once pushed locks the puzzle, and a box panel that's fatal if left open. With only four lives that added up fast. Some of it was my own carelessness, like sending several commands at once at turn 206.

interestingness.why: Time travel where history really changes (the jewel room is bare afterwards), a viewing table that teleports you, an old man whose belongings you rebuild piece by piece, and a final reveal of your own face. Ambitious and coherent.

prose.why: Wry, melancholy and exact. Long examine texts paid off almost every time, and the timed lines on the ledge were superb. Some of the lake and repellent hints ran long and over-explained, but I was glad of them.
